diagnostic_evidence.quote: The problem of learning $\spec_{\mathrm{ap}}(\mathcal{K}_F)$ from $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{N}}$ for $F\in\Omega_{\mathbb{N}}$ lies in $\Pi_3$ and has $\mathrm{SCI}=3$.

Let $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{N}$ (or any countable discrete space), equipped with the usual counting measure $\omega=\sum_{j=1}^\infty \delta_j$, and consider dynamical systems governed by a nonlinear function $F:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow \mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$.

Such discrete-space systems are well studied since they are often conjugate to chaotic systems on continuous spaces; hence, we may also translate computational problems and classifications to continuous spaces.

Here, the statespace is a compact metric space $(\mathcal{X},d_{\mathcal{X}})$, $x\in\mathcal{X}$ is the system's state, $F:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}$ is an \textit{unknown} continuous function

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that computing spectra for general systems (the class $\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}$ of continuous maps on a compact metric space with finite Borel measure, as in Theorem 2) requires three limits and hence Theorem 2's tower is optimal. The only lower bound proved (thm3/thm:discrete_space) concerns a different computational problem: statespace $\mathbb{N}$ (non-compact, infinite counting measure), maps into $\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}$ with no continuity, and a different evaluation set. No embedding of this problem into the compact continuous setting is given; the sentence about conjugacy to chaotic systems is not an argument. Thus $\mathrm{SCI}\geq 3$ for $\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}$ and the optimality of Theorem 2's third limit are unsupported.

failure_location.quote: Generically, this cannot be achieved in two limits. Hence, \cref{thm2}'s algorithm is optimal.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the optimality/sharpness claim to the discrete-space problem actually treated in thm3, or supply a construction embedding the combinatorial problem into continuous maps on a compact metric space with a finite measure.
issues.overall_effect: The sharpness/optimality claims for the three-limit tower of thm2 on compact continuous systems (summary bullet, SCI-for-Koopman paragraph, fig:SCI1) are unsupported; thm3 itself is unaffected.

Moreover, intersecting the two classes with the two-limit classifications $\Pi_2$ (for $\Omega^\alpha$) and $\Sigma_2$ (for $\Omega^m$) yields only $\Sigma_2\cap\Pi_2$, not $\Sigma_1\cap\Pi_1$. The paragraph also calls $\Sigma_1$ 'stronger' than $\Sigma_1\cap\Pi_1$, which is backwards. The correct $\Sigma_1$ classification of the intersection is proved independently in thm:general_koopman_computation, so only this prose is wrong.

issues.failure_explanation: Membership in $\Omega^\delta_{[0,1]}$ requires both $a_n\le 1+\delta$ and $a_n^{-1}\le 1+\delta$ for all $n$. At the junction the ratio is $a_{N}=r_1(1-r_2)/(1-r_1)$ (or with $r_1,r_2$ swapped), so $(F_c^{-1})'=a_N^{-1}=(1-r_1)/(r_1(1-r_2))$ on $S_{N+1}$. Only $a_N\le(1-r_2)/(1-r_1)$ is checked; the reciprocal is not controlled by (deriv_bound). Example: $\delta=1$, $r_1=1/2$, $r_2=3/4$ satisfies (deriv_bound) but gives $(F_c^{-1})'=4>1+\delta$. Hence the adversarial maps need not lie in the class as constructed.

failure_location.quote: It follows from the bound \cref{deriv_bound}, that $F_{c^{(2)}}\in \Omega_{[0,1]}^{\delta}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the conditions on $r_1,r_2$ to also require $(1-r_1)/(r_1(1-r_2))\le 1+\delta$ and $(1-r_2)/(r_2(1-r_1))\le 1+\delta$; such $r_1<r_2$ with (sep_bound) exist for every $\delta>0$ (e.g. $r_1$ slightly above $1/(1+\delta)$ and $r_2$ slightly above $r_1$).
issues.overall_effect: The verification that each $F_{c^{(k)}}$ and the limit $F_c$ lie in $\Omega^\delta_{[0,1]}$ is incomplete; the lower bound argument otherwise stands.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: and the proof is almost identical when restricting to smooth functions in $\Omega_{[0,1]}^{\delta}$.
Let $\hat r_j=r_2$ if $j$ is even and $\hat r_j=r_1$ if $j$ is odd.
We consider (smoothed) interval exchange maps, whose derivatives switch in a self-similar manner at the endpoints of the interval.

issues.failure_explanation: Any map in the construction satisfies $F(c_n)=c_{n+1}$ with $c_n\to 1$, so by the mean value theorem $F'$ takes the value $a_n=|S_{n+1}|/|S_n|$ at some point of $S_n$. The adversarial sequence $c$ is built so that $a_n$ alternates between $r_1$ and $r_2$ over ever longer stretches, hence $a_n$ has no limit and $F'$ cannot be continuous at $1$ (similarly at $0$). Thus no smoothing of $F_c$ is $C^1$ on the closed interval $[0,1]$, and the claimed 'almost identical' proof for smooth functions only covers maps smooth on the open interval. The main-text class $\Omega_{[0,1]}$ ('F smooth') is therefore not shown to admit the lower bound if smoothness on $[0,1]$ is meant.

failure_location.quote: Moreover, the same classifications hold when restricting to smooth functions in $\Omega_{[0,1]}^{\delta}$, or when restricting to piecewise affine functions in $\Omega_{[0,1]}^{\delta}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the smooth clause (and $\Omega_{[0,1]}$ in thm1) as maps that are smooth on the open interval $(0,1)$ with $F,F^{-1}$ Lipschitz (or piecewise smooth as in $\Omega^\delta_{[0,1]}$); a proof for globally $C^1$ maps would require a different mechanism than alternating $a_n$.
issues.overall_effect: The lower bound of thm:interval/thm1 for smooth maps is only established for maps smooth on $(0,1)$ (piecewise smooth with Lipschitz bounds), not for $C^1([0,1])$ maps.
issues.title: Extension of the interval lower bound to globally smooth maps is unsupported: the adversarial map cannot be C^1 at the endpoint
issues.why_classification: The advertised scope must be narrowed to exclude globally smooth maps on the closed interval, but a closely comparable lower bound (interior-smooth Lipschitz maps) is fully supported by the existing argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For (a), note that the map $F$ is $C^0$ conjugate to $G(x,y)=(x,y+x)$.
In the above construction, we switched between $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}(F_{f^{(k)}})=0$ for $k$ odd and $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}(F_{f^{(k)}})=1$ for $k$ even.

issues.failure_explanation: For the skew product $F(x,y)=(x,y+f(x))$, every $g(x,y)=h(x)$ satisfies $\mathcal{K}_F g=g$; taking $h$ with zero mean gives eigenfunctions (eigenvalue 1) in $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$ with spectral measure a point mass at $1$. Hence part (a) is false, and the system is not even ergodic, let alone weakly mixing. (The proof's claim of $C^0$ conjugacy to $G(x,y)=(x,y+x)$ also fails since $f$ is symmetric, hence not injective.) Consequently $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}(F_{f^{(k)}})=1$ for every $k$, both odd and even, so the alternating construction does not produce the claimed switching and the proof that $\{\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}},\Omega_p\}\notin\Delta_2^{\mathbb{P}}$ (and the first statement of thm4, 'existence of a non-trivial eigenfunction' with non-trivial defined as lying in $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$) collapses. The $\Xi_p$ (pure point spectrum) part survives because the only eigenvalue of $F_{f^{(1)}}$ is $1$ (Fourier expansion in $y$ shows eigenvalue $\lambda\ne1$ would force $g_k$ supported where $e^{ikf(x)}=\lambda$, a null set for strictly monotone $f$), so $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{pp}}=\{1\}$ still alternates with $\mathbb{T}$.

failure_location.quote: If $f$ is strictly increasing on $[-\pi,0]$, the spectral measure of $\mathcal{K}_F$ with respect to any $g\in L^2(\mathcal{X},\omega)$ is continuous on $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$. It follows that there are no eigenfunctions in the subspace $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct Lemma (a) to state only that $1$ is the sole eigenvalue (no eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $\ne1$), and redefine the decision problem as 'does $\mathcal{K}_F$ have an eigenvalue other than $1$' (equivalently $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{pp}}\ne\{1\}$); the existing $\Xi_p$ construction then gives the $\Delta_2^{\mathbb{P}}$ lower bound and the $\Sigma_2$ tower for $\Xi_p$ yields the upper bound. A lower bound for weak-mixing detection as literally stated would need a new (ergodic) adversarial family.
issues.overall_effect: The decision-problem lower bound (detecting non-trivial eigenfunctions / weak mixing) in thm:torus and the first impossibility statement of thm4 are unproved; the pure-point-spectrum lower bound and the upper bounds are unaffected.
issues.title: Lemma technical_lemma3(a) is false (skew products have invariant functions of x), so the lower bound for detecting non-trivial eigenfunctions is unproved
issues.why_classification: A stated formal result is false and a main-text impossibility claim loses its literal form, but a recognizably comparable result (undecidability of eigenvalues other than 1 in one limit) is recoverable from the existing construction with a contained modification.
